solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cut off source of exclusive rum (8)

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone is refused a supply of a rare, exclusive rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink, but it is the old British adjective meaning odd.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to be cut off from family or friends is to be alienated from them, the sense in 'an estranged son'.

clue.text: Zany dance for prison guards? (9)

blocks.note: a screw is British slang for a prison officer
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A daft dance put on for the warders of a jail.
explanation.walkthrough: A dance for screws would be a screws' ball, which gives the answer; 'screw' for a prison officer is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Screwball is an adjective as well as a noun: zany, crazily eccentric.

clue.text: What one may do after a fault in supply (7)

definitions.text: What one may do after a fault

blocks.clueFragment: What one may do after a fault
blocks.note: a tennis fault: the player gets to deliver the ball a second time
a stock held back for later use

explanation.surface: Advice on what to do once a flaw turns up in the supply chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fault' sounds like a defect in goods; it is the tennis fault, after which the server serves again: RE-SERVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: in tennis a faulted first serve is followed by a second, a serving again; and a stock kept back is a supply in store.

clue.text: No TV clergyman is famous (5)

blocks.note: Father Ted, the priest in the Irish TV sitcom

explanation.surface: A claim that no clergyman on television is a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Ted was a popular sitcom about three priests on an Irish island.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means well known, famous.

clue.text: Reveal oddly chopped fish (3)

indicators.note: the odd letters are chopped off, leaving the even ones

blocks.note: rEvEaL with R, V, A removed

explanation.surface: An order to show off a fish that has been cut up strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' usually means keep the odd letters; here they are what gets chopped, so the even letters stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the long snake-like swimmer of rivers and seas is a fish, a crossword regular because of its three handy letters.

clue.text: Psychologist with case for live dance music (6)

indicators.note: a word's case is its outside, the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A psychologist making the argument for live dance music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case for' reads as an argument in favour; it is the shell of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Jungle is a fast, bass-heavy style of dance music from 1990s Britain.

clue.text: Post office? (3,6)

blocks.note: the surface pushes mail; the setter means a post as in a job or position
a public office where those posts are advertised and filled; the question mark flags the pun

explanation.walkthrough: A post is a job, so a 'post office' is where jobs are handed out; a Jobcentre is the British government office for jobseekers.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on 'post': the British state office for the unemployed deals in posts meaning jobs, not letters.

clue.text: One messiah maybe held up around old city (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, held up means read bottom to top
one thing placed around another encloses it, so BRIAN is split to hold O

blocks.note: Brian, mistaken for the messiah in Monty Python's Life of Brian

explanation.surface: A would-be messiah stopped on the road near an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's not the Messiah' is the famous line about Brian in Life of Brian, hence the 'maybe'. I + B(O)RIAN reads IBORIAN, which turned up is NAIROBI.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Kenyan capital is one of many cities the bare word could point to.

clue.text: Run on the level (5)

blocks.note: to run off, in British slang: two words, use your legs
honest, above board: the clipped form of 'legitimate'

explanation.surface: A sprint over flat ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg it' is British slang for run off, and 'legit' is short for legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: Two slang senses: British 'leg it' means make a run for it, and the clipped adjective means genuine, on the level.

clue.text: I recalled teacher is pupil’s neighbour (4)

indicators.note: called back, so read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone remembers that the teacher lives next door to a pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: The pupil is the one in the eye, not the classroom, which the teacher pushes you towards.
explanation.definitionFit: The iris is the coloured ring right around the pupil of the eye.

clue.text: To free drill, beg for costly spanner? (4,6)

indicators.note: the letters of 'drill, beg' are set free to rearrange

explanation.surface: A plea for a pricey spanner to release a stuck drill, as in a workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: A spanner sounds like a tool beside the drill, but here it is something that spans a river; charging to cross makes it costly.
explanation.definitionFit: A toll bridge spans a gap and costs you money to cross.

clue.text: Rioting crowd ends a cutting-edge show (5,5)

indicators.note: the letters run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: A riotous mob brings a trendy performance to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting-edge' sounds like avant-garde, but the show literally involves blades.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword dance is a performance over or with swords, so it has cutting edges.

clue.text: Heads for vegetarian food? (7)

blocks.note: loaf = head, from rhyming slang loaf of bread

explanation.surface: A question about what vegetarians like to eat, or which way their heads turn.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Heads' supplies two slang words for head: nut, and loaf from Cockney rhyming slang (loaf of bread = head).
explanation.definitionFit: A nut loaf is a vegetarian roast made from nuts.

clue.text: Word of advice — try harder at first (4)

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: of advice — try harder at first
blocks.note: first letters of Of Advice Try Harder

explanation.surface: A piece of counsel: just try harder from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Word of advice' looks like one phrase; the definition is only 'Word', and 'of' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath is a solemn word, as in giving your word.

clue.text: Hard material covering a small window (8)

indicators.note: CEMENT covers, goes around, A and S

blocks.note: s = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A tough substance laid over a little window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small window' reads as the definition, but 'small' is S and only 'window' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a side-hinged window that opens outward like a door is one particular kind of window.

clue.text: Flog spare pots, one has a chip (1-8)

indicators.note: flog = beat, so the letters are knocked about

explanation.surface: Sell off the extra crockery, since one of the pots is chipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flog' reads as sell, which fits the spare pots; here it means beat, and 'chip' is a microchip, not a crack.
explanation.definitionFit: An e-passport carries an electronic chip holding the holder's details.

clue.text: New T-shirt is long (6)

indicators.note: a new version of the letters

explanation.surface: A complaint that a brand-new T-shirt is too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' reads as an adjective about the shirt; it is the verb, to long for something.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to crave something, as in thirsting for knowledge, is to long for it.

clue.text: Flights here reportedly look all right (9)

indicators.note: as it would be reported, i.e. spoken

explanation.surface: At the airport, the planes seem to be doing fine, so the reports say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flights' suggests aircraft; these are flights of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A stairwell is the shaft in a building where the flights of stairs are.

clue.text: Dad’s ringing large old lady for vital matter? (6)

indicators.note: PA'S forms a ring around L

blocks.note: l = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Dad phones his elderly mother about something important.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' looks like making a phone call; it is PA'S encircling L. 'Old lady' is slang for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Plasma is the fluid part of blood, so matter vital to life; it is also a state of matter.

clue.text: Nick what capable people are up to (7)

definitions.text: what capable people are up to

blocks.note: a small cut or mark on a surface

blocks.clueFragment: what capable people are up to
blocks.note: the idiom 'up to ...' meaning good enough; originally the line boxers had to reach

explanation.surface: Asking what competent people get up to when they steal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' can mean steal (British informal), which pushes the surface towards crime; here it is a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a nick is a small surface mark, and the idiom for meeting the required standard ends with this word.

clue.text: In foreign parts, manages broadcast (8)

indicators.note: put out over the air, so spoken

explanation.surface: Someone runs a broadcasting operation abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' sits as though it is what is being managed; it is the sound instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverbial synonym: across the sea, abroad, is where foreign parts lie for someone in Britain.

clue.text: Leading group in Home Counties of highest status (7)

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so SE opens up to hold UP and REM

blocks.note: SE = the South East, where the Home Counties are; S is its first half

explanation.surface: The top band in the counties around London, and so the best of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London, in the South East of England, abbreviated SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: top-ranking, as in a supreme commander or court, is of highest status.

clue.text: Place to relax before boxer’s last fight (4)

indicators.note: the final letter of boxer

blocks.note: a spa is a place to unwind

explanation.surface: A boxer unwinds somewhere before the final bout of their career.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxer and 'fight' belong together, but only 'fight' defines; the boxer gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: boxers trade practice punches, and people argue, both a kind of fight.

clue.text: God’s power curtailed southern town (5)

indicators.note: its tail, the last letter, is cut off

explanation.surface: A deity's might was cut back in a town in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curtailed' seems to go with power, but it trims the town. Luton is a town just north of London, so southern from a British view.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Roman ruler of the underworld, Hades to the Greeks, is one god among many.

clue.text: Attraction of drink consuming a distant ship (6,4)

indicators.note: to consume is to swallow, so the drink takes the other letters inside itself

blocks.note: a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: The allure of drinking on board a far-off ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attraction' sounds like allure, but it is a tourist attraction. S(A FAR)IP + ARK.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari park is a tourist attraction where animals roam and visitors drive through.

clue.text: Transmit again about unfinished letter (5)

indicators.note: the last letter is left off

blocks.note: RUNE, an old alphabet letter, without its E

explanation.surface: Sending a message again because a letter was left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' suggests correspondence; it is a character of an alphabet, a rune.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcasting verb: showing a programme a second time, a repeat, is transmitting it again.

clue.text: One with lots of fresh European Cointreau (10)

indicators.note: a fresh arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: Someone with plenty of new French orange liqueur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots' reads as plenty; it means the items sold at an auction.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic-leaning description: the person at the saleroom rostrum handles numbered lots, items put up for bidding.

clue.text: Consume centres of ten roast pasties (3)

indicators.note: take the middle letter of each word

explanation.surface: An invitation to eat the middles of ten roasted pasties.
explanation.walkthrough: A pasty is a pastry turnover with a savoury filling, a Cornish speciality.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: taking food in, as with the pasties of the surface, is consuming it.

clue.text: Steady revenue is somewhat reduced (4)

indicators.note: the word revenue is cut down to a part of itself

explanation.surface: Income has held steady, though it has dipped a little.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a financial report; 'reduced' reads as a fall in income but tells you to cut revenue down.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective synonym: regular and unvarying, like a steady pace or an even keel.

clue.text: Farm animal with headgear is big deal (2,4)

blocks.note: a sow is a female pig

explanation.surface: A pig in a hat is quite an event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big deal' is said sarcastically, meaning it doesn't matter, just like 'so what'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Big deal!' and 'So what?' both dismiss something as unimportant.

clue.text: Present lady’s coat in a gentle way (8)

indicators.note: a word's coat is its outside, the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Handing a woman her coat with care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as a gift; it is the verb, to tender or offer.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb synonym: acting with loving care and softness is behaving in a gentle way.
